Paleomagnetic samples were collected from six of the Bonin Islands located on the northeastern margin (27’N, 142’E) of the Philippine Sea. These volcanic islands are of Eocene age. Both lava flows and dikes were collected at each of 34 sites with Chichi-jima the largest island being sampled most extensively. Mean directions of the 27 sites on Chichi-jima are divisible into two groups showing antipolar relationships at the 95% confidence level. A between-site mean direction after tilt correction of 22 of the 27 sites is I = 7”, D = 1 lo’, ass = 14’ while that of the remaining sites is I = lo”, D = 273”, c+s = 32’. The seven sites on the other three Benin Islands, as a whole, seem to cluster well around the mean of I = 3”. D = 213” with us5 = 19”, which differs significantly from both mean directions determined for Chichi-jima. The low inclinations and deflected declinations of the Bonin Islands are interpreted as being due to tectonic rotation. The islands have undergone a northward migration of at least 30” from the equatorial region together with (possibly clockwise) rotation of 30” to over 90” around the vertical axis. Previous studies (e.g., Louden, 1977) suggested that the nearby Philip- pine Sea plate drifted northward from the equatorial region and rotated clockwise by several tens of degrees. Plate movements of the subducting Pacific plate could have 21 produced additional displacements. Paleomagnetic work in several of the Bonin Islands was begun in 1980 in order to examine the validity of the tectonic movements suggested in previous models. Sampling was conducted on three Bonin Islands, namely Chichi-jima, Ani-jima and Ototo-jima. The paleomagnetic results from Chichi-jima, the geologically best known of the Bonin Islands are presented here together with the preliminary paleomagnetic data for the other Bonin Islands (Kodama, 1981). Results for the islands, Ani-jima and Ototo-jima, will be published elsewhere in the near future. section_candidates.excerpt: BONIN ISLANDS The Bonin Islands consist of three groups of islands, each group lying about 50 km apart (Fig. 1). Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. Kikuchi (1890) first reported the characteristic pyroxene components in volcanic rocks on Chichi-jima. Peterson (189 1) gave the name “ boninite” to these andesitic rocks rich in bronzite phenocrysts. The rare volcanic rock called “boninite”, a vesicular two pyroxene feldspar-free glassy andesite with a high content of MgO (6612%) (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977), occurs as the main constituent of the oldest volcanic events in the Bonin Islands. No volcanic rock exactly equivalent to the boninite has yet been found elsewhere (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977) although similar rocks have been reported recently for the fore-arc region of the Marianas (Hussong et al., 1978). Early in this century paleontological studies of the Nummulites from Haha-jima were carried out by such workers as Yoshiwara (1902), Yabe (1920) and Hanzawa (1925). Previous studies (e.g., Louden, 1977) suggested that the nearby Philip- pine Sea plate drifted northward from the equatorial region and rotated clockwise by several tens of degrees. Plate movements of the subducting Pacific plate could have 21 produced additional displacements. Paleomagnetic work in several of the Bonin Islands was begun in 1980 in order to examine the validity of the tectonic movements suggested in previous models. Sampling was conducted on three Bonin Islands, namely Chichi-jima, Ani-jima and Ototo-jima. The paleomagnetic results from Chichi-jima, the geologically best known of the Bonin Islands are presented here together with the preliminary paleomagnetic data for the other Bonin Islands (Kodama, 1981). Results for the islands, Ani-jima and Ototo-jima, will be published elsewhere in the near future. section_candidates.excerpt: BONIN ISLANDS The Bonin Islands consist of three groups of islands, each group lying about 50 km apart (Fig. 1). Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. Kikuchi (1890) first reported the characteristic pyroxene components in volcanic rocks on Chichi-jima. Peterson (189 1) gave the name “ boninite” to these andesitic rocks rich in bronzite phenocrysts. The rare volcanic rock called “boninite”, a vesicular two pyroxene feldspar-free glassy andesite with a high content of MgO (6612%) (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977), occurs as the main constituent of the oldest volcanic events in the Bonin Islands. No volcanic rock exactly equivalent to the boninite has yet been found elsewhere (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977) although similar rocks have been reported recently for the fore-arc region of the Marianas (Hussong et al., 1978). Early in this century paleontological studies of the Nummulites from Haha-jima were carried out by such workers as Yoshiwara (1902), Yabe (1920) and Hanzawa (1925). Because of the subsequent loop in this curve, the possibility of an age of around 800 m.y. cannot be ex- cluded, but in any case the Raggedy Mountain Group was emplaced in Precambrian time. (3) A locality near the contact with Cambrian granites was probably remagnetized in Cambrian time, at temperatures in ex- cess of 450 ø . Symons Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada, N9B 3P4 Abstract. The 142 Ma old Jurassic Topley Intrusions are exposed in the middle of the Intermontane Belt or Stikinia subterrane of composite Terrane I of the Canadian Cordillera in central British Columbia. Thermal demagneti- zation at 560øC leads to the isolation of a single stable magnetic component directed at 324'2ø' 54'1ø' 95 = 8'6ø in 17 of the 22 sites. The pole position of 238,2øW, 58.4øN, p = 8.3 ø , a m = 11.8 ø for the component is discordant relative to the North American craton. This position supports previous work in suggesting that Stikinia has been translated northward by 14 + 2 ø or about 1400 km between mid-Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time. It also suggests that the central portion of Stikinia has not been rotated about a vertical axis by a statistically signifi- cant amount whereas minor marginal blocks of the subterrane have been subjected to large and variable amounts of both clockwise and counter- clockwise rotation. Introduction and Geologic Setting The nature and origin of the paleomagnetism in carbonate rocks have received considerable attention over the past decade [e.g., Lowrie and Alvarez, 1977; Heller and Channell, 1979; Lowrie and Heller, 1982; McCabe et al., 1983a]. Paleo- magnetic data have constrained the ages of events affecting carbonates, such as regional dolomitization, base metal mineralization, and oxidation [e.g., Wu and Beales, 1981; Shanks et al., 1979; McCabe et al., 1983a; Wisniowiecki et al., 1983; Channell et al., 1982]. It has been shown that the major carriers of the magne- tization may be diagenetic in origin McCabe et al., 1983a,b]. We have examined aspects of the Leadville Formation (Kinderhookean-Osagean) of Central Colorado. The Leadville Formation offers an opportunity to st

As relief is considerable in the region, fresh, unweathered material was readily available. All samples were collected by orienting blocks (independent measurements) in the field using a magnetic compass; standard specimens were pre- pared in the laboratory. We employed a spinner magnetometer, on which was attached a 500 count/ rotation optical shaft encoder. Signal analysis and data acquisition were carried out using an interfaced microprocessor. The instrument has a sensitivity of better than 1 x 10 -4 A/m; this is adequate to resolve almost all significant com- ponents during demagnetization. Orthogonal de- magnetization diagrams and vector subtraction techniques were used to calculate component di- rections. Extraction of magnetic material for Curie temperature analysis and SEM inspection followed the methods of McCabe et al. 983a] and Wisniowiecki et al. [1983]. In the laboratory, samples were cored and standard paleomagnetic specimens prepared. Some of the samples were set aside for rock magnetic or dissolu- tion experiments. Specimens were demagnetized in the laboratory using both AF and therma] treatments and measured with an ScT cryogenic magnetometer. Each specimen was demagnetized in stepwise fashion. The demagnetization data were plotted on orthogonal de- magnetization diagrams and the directions of the component magnetizations were determined by vector subtraction (ZijderveId, 1967). The magnetic fraction of the insoluble residue was extracted from a water suspen- sion with a home-built magnetic extractor. The Trenton Limestone in New York State has been the object of at least two previous paleomag- netic investigations. Graham (1954, 1956) reported well-clustered natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions that have a mean declination/inclination of ]790/+82 o. McElhinny and Opdyke (]973) resampled the same section at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- za

ion at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- zation, are contaminated with a component of rema- nence aligned with the present-day magnetic field. After alternating field (AF) demagnetization they found a mean direction of 173o/+18o. Further, they showed (as had Graham) that the magnetization was acquired after a syndepositional slump but that the minimum and maximum axes of magnetic suscepti- bility anisotropy show a typically sedimentary fabric. They concluded that the magnetization was due to early post-depositional reorientation of the magnetite carrier grains in the ambient Ordovician field. The paleo- magnetic pole is located at 53.00 N, 126.9o E (K=97.7; A-95=2.7o). This pole is plotted in Fig. 5 along with the pole found by McElhinny and Opdyke (1973). It is clear from the figure that the pole we have obtained is near Late Carboniferous and Early Permian poles for North America but is not at all close to other Ordovician poles, indicating remagnetization in the Late Paleozoic. This new Trenton pole is close to the Onondaga Limestone pole (Kent, 1979) which failed the fold test. It is also virtually coincident with the remagnetized Helderberg Limestone pole reported by Scotese et al. (1982). A fold test on the Helderberg magnetization (McCabe et al., 1983)demonstrated a syn-Alleghenian acquisition of the characteristic remanence and proved its secondary nature. The Trenton thus appears also to carry a Late Paleozoic secondary magnetization. Introduction Sedimentary carbonates of Trentonian age form one of the most widespread rock units in North America. The Trenton Limestone in New York State has been the object of at least two previous paleomag- netic investigations. Graham (1954, 1956) reported well-clustered natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions that have a mean declination/inclination of ]790/+82 o. McElhinny and Opdyke (]973) resampled the same section at Trenton Falls, New York that was sampled by Graham. They showed that Graham's results, which were obtained without any demagneti- zation, are contaminated with a component of rema- nence aligned with the present-day magnetic field. After alternating field (AF) demagnetization they found a mean direction of 173o/+18o. Further, they showed (as had Graham) that the magnetization was acquired after a syndepositional slump but that the minimum and maximum axes of magnetic suscepti- bility anisotropy show a typically sedimentary fabric. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Abstract. Samples for paleomagnetic study were collected from the area of Red Sandstone Creek (Lat. 39.73øN, Long. 253.6) near Vail, Colorado, in hopes of locating the stratigraphic base of the Kiaman Reversed Interval to within a few meters. Previous workers had sampled the same upper Pennsylvanian and Permian Minturn and Maroon Formations in this section and had placed the base of the Kiaman at 91m to 213m above the Minturn Formation. The interval from 276m below to 420m above the Maroon/Minturn contact was sampled in the present study at one meter intervals where possible. Of the 171 samples collected, only 2 had near normal components. The 2 were not consecutive and the normal components were removed easily by thermal cleaning or were shown to be a viscous overprint of the present field. The previous workers were apparently misled by a lack of magnetic cleaning of their samples. The conclusion of this study is that the base of the Kiaman must be stratigraphically lower in this section. The pole position from the sampled section is Lat. 42.6øN, Long. 115.4øE, A95=2.75 for N=145 samples. Introduction In what is now the southern Canadian Cordillera, the first oceanic terrane to be emplaced against the ancient continental margin of western North America (now the Omineca Belt) in the early Mesozoic was Terrane I (Figure 1; Monger et al., 1982; Monger, 1984). Terrane I is a composite of several smaller terranes, one of which is the Quesnel terrane. Paleomagnetic results from the Quesnel terrane are described. The Quesnel terrane, as part of Terrane I, was thrust onto the Omineca Belt in the late Early Jurassic, and together they were deformed, metamorphosed, and intruded by syn- to post- tectonic plutons in the Middle to Late Jurassic (Read and Wheeler, 1976; Archibald et al., 1983; Brown et al., 1985). Introduction During historic time, both the amount of secular variation of the Earth's magnetic field (SV) and the magnitude of the nondipole field, whose changes cause most of the historically observed secular variation, have been rather irregularly distributed over the earth's surface [Cox and Doe11, 1964; Doe11 and Cox, 1972]. These features are at the present time of larger magnitude in the Southern Hemisphere than in the Northern Hemisphere and are almost completely lacking in the central Pacific region [Doe11 and Cox, 1962; McWilliams et al., 1981]. As a result of evidence from Hawaii that suggested a sustained interval of low geomagnetic secular variation, analogous studies were conducted elsewhere in the Pacific on the Galapagos [Doe11 and Cox, 1961], on Easter Island [Issacson and Heinrichs, 1976], and in the Society Islands [Duncan, 1975]. These studies showed secular variation consistent with a \"standard\" model of global variation based upon modern dipole and nondipole fields [Cox, 1970; McWilliams et al., 1981] and hence the region of anomalously low secular variation has been constrained to smaller regions of the Pacific. Introduction In the last few years different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolution of this area. Some of these models (Brunn, 1976; Tapponnier, 1977) assume that the deformation is entirely related to the main Tertiary Alpine phase and is thus completed before the neotectonic period. However, many recent tectonic, paleomagnetic and geophysical studies have led to the recognition of the extreme mobility of the Aegean lithosphere (McKenzie, 1978; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Laj et al., 1982; Horner and Freeman, 1983; Kondopoulou et Lauer, 1984; Kissel et al., 1985; 1986a,b). According to these authors this movement is at first approximation a 30 ø clockwise rotation of a semi-rigid plate about a pole situated near 40øN; 18øE in the southern Adriatic Sea. A large back-arc distension, up to about 70%, is superimposed to this rotation loc- ally modifying its value which is maximum in the northwestern region and progressively decreases eastward to attain zero near the Anatolian coast. Aegea cannot thus be considered as a rigid plate. The extent of the deformation has led Mercier (1977) and Mercier et al., (1979) to consider Aegea as the plastically deformed edge of the Eurasiatic plate, with movement occurring along slip lines as suggested by Tapponnier (1977). Introduction In the last few years different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolution of this area. Some of these models (Brunn, 1976; Tapponnier, 1977) assume that the deformation is entirely related to the main Tertiary Alpine phase and is thus completed before the neotectonic period. However, many recent tectonic, paleomagnetic and geophysical studies have led to the recognition of the extreme mobility of the Aegean lithosphere (McKenzie, 1978; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Laj et al., 1982; Horner and Freeman, 1983; Kondopoulou et Lauer, 1984; Kissel et al., 1985; 1986a,b). ng grabens and troughs. The neotectonic period is also characterized in this region by a dextral strike-slip motion along the north Anatolian fault the western termination of which is located north of Evia. In northern and central Aegea widespread calc-alkaline activity occurred, belonging to two different phases of volcanic activity of Oligo-Miocene and Plio-Quaternary age separated by a period of quiescence of several million years (Bellon et al., 1979; Fytikas et al., 1984). In addition to these calc-alkaline products, small volumes of lava with variable petrogenetic character were emitted over all central Aegea. Sedimentary formations are also present and essentially constituted by continental (fluvio-lacustrine) and brackish limestones and marls which indicate the quasi-definitive emersion of these regions. Sites were sampled in volcanic and sedimentary formations in the islands of central Aegea (Evia, Skyros, Alonissos) and from the Volos region. The geographical location of these sites is indicated in the schematic map of Figure 1. Introduction As a result of the indracontinental convergence in Eastern Turkey, most of Turkey moved westward along the North and East Anatolian strike-slip faults. Since at least late Miocene, this motion is accompanied by large scale N-S extension in the Aegean and in Western Turkey with complementary E-W shortening (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1981; Angelier et al., 1981) . In this paper we report paleomagnetic data from northeastern Aegea showing that significant rotations of adjacent coherent blocks about vertical axes and in opposite senses have occurred in this region since at most 20 m.y. Although the data are still incomplete, the complicated rotational pattern in this area is easier to describe in terms of local rotations than in the framework of the general westward movement of the \"Anatolian Plate\" resulting from the Eurasia-Arabia collision (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). Geological Setting and Sampling The studied area and the location of the sampling sites are shown in Figure 1. Introduction As a result of the indracontinental convergence in Eastern Turkey, most of Turkey moved westward along the North and East Anatolian strike-slip faults. Since at least late Miocene, this motion is accompanied by large scale N-S extension in the Aegean and in Western Turkey with complementary E-W shortening (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979; Mercier et al., 1979; Le Pichon and Angelier, 1981; Angelier et al., 1981) . In this paper we report paleomagnetic data from northeastern Aegea showing that significant rotations of adjacent coherent blocks about vertical axes and in opposite senses have occurred in this region since at most 20 m.y. Although the data are still incomplete, the complicated rotational pattern in this area is easier to describe in terms of local rotations than in the framework of the general westward movement of the \"Anatolian Plate\" resulting from the Eurasia-Arabia collision (Tapponnier, 1977; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). Geological Setting and Sampling The studied area and the location of the sampling sites are shown in Figure 1. The most striking structural and morphological features of this region re the E-W and NNE trending grabens (McKenzie, 1978; Dewey and eng6r, 1979). Focal m

Focal mechanism solutions obtained from the Alasehir and Gediz grabens, have shown that motion takes place on faults of listric geometry (Eyidoan and Jackson, 1985). The NNE faults are probably partially inherited from Neo-Tethyan-structures while the E-W fault system corresponds to a neotectonic structural direction. The complex pattern of faulting includes numerous other neotectonic faults of various orientations and displacements (Kaya, 1981), most of which are truncated by younger faults of different orientations. Slickensides indicating strike-slip movements in opposite senses and in different directions are also frequently observed in the field. This paleomagnetic study of =700 specimens yielded a normal segment in all 5 profiles and an excursive segment in 3 pro- files. The normal zones give, in most cases, significantly different directions which sug- gests that they are not strictly coeval and that deposition rates in this till are highly variable from one point to the next. Overall, they give a virtual geomagnetic pole located at 273.1øW, 73.0øN (p = 1.7 , am = 2.6). Simi- larly the 3 excursive zones are not exactly coeval. Assuming the remanence reflects a single excursion then the pole appears to swing from mid-Africa to mid-South Pacific, and then back to the normal Arctic pole. This polar sequence and the apparent paleofield intensi- ties are notably similar to those found in aboriginal fireplaces at Lake Mungo, Australia. The Meadowcliffe Till is the first Ontario till to yield evidence of recording a geomag- netic field excursion(s). Accordingly its pa- leomagnetic age is set at 30,500 + 1,500 yr B.P. which is within the 8,000 yr window per- mitted by the single radiocarbon dates from below and above the till. Lower Devonian volcanic rocks from Chapman syncline near Presque Isle, Maine yield paleomagnetic directions unlike those determined for stable North America. Sites in four differ- ent igneous units of the Dockendorff Group give a pole position of 24 ø N latitude and 132 ø E longitude. These rocks are unmetamorphosed, and appear to be unaffected by the mid-Devonian Acadian orogeny. The pole agrees with other published data for upper Devonian rocks of eas- tern New England and the Canadian Maritimes. This indicates that the Avalon microcontinent may have extended

ine. These rocks were chosen for: 1) their position between the stable plat- form and the alleged microcontinent, 2) their age prior to the Acadian orogeny, but non-invol- vement in the orogeny, and 3) their present unal- tered state. Geologic Setting Northern Maine was an area of deposition from middle Ordovician to early Devonian, with spor- adic volcanics within the sedimentary sequence. All but the youngest strata are weakly metamor- phosed, with abundant fossils retained, which allows for dating and interpretation of Paleozoic units not well understood in the rest of the Nor- thern Appalachians [Boucot, 1968]. Introduction The Klamath Mountains province of northern California and southern Oregon consists of a series of ophiolitic fragments and volcanic island arcs that formed during Paleozoic and Mesozoic times. Available paleomagnetic evidence indicates that some Devonian to Jurassic rocks of the Klamath Mountains have undergone large rota- tions relative to a stable North America since their formation [Achache et al., 1982; Fagin and Gose, 1983; Schultz, 1983; Mankinen et al., 1984; Bogen, 1986]. A paleomagnetic study of super- jacent Cretaceous strata of the Klamath Mountains [Mankinen and Irwin, 1982] indicated that little or no rotation of the province had occurred since Cretaceous time and perhaps not since Early Cretaceous. No paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant latitudinal displacements has been found for any of the Klamath terranes. Plutons of the Shasta Bally belt intrude mainly the Eastern Klamath and Central Metamorphic terranes. During the 1979-80 field season, a major field programme in the Ellsworth Mountains was conducted by the US Antarctic Research Program 9 , which included a systematic palaeomag­ netic collection of the Cambrian to Devonian sedimentary section . Beforehand, the magnetic remanence of a suite of unoriented samples collected by expeditions during the early 1960s was investigated by stepwise alternating field and thermal demagnetization and plotting the results on the orthogonal projections of Zijderveld 10• Promising lithologies were identified on the basis of linear trajectories on the projections 11 , consistency of directions within a given sample and the physical properties of the remanence, such as coercivity and blocking temperature consistent with single-domain carriers.
